issues.issue: Condominium and PUD eligibility is measured by the "HELOC Seller's eligibility requirements as set forth in HELOC Seller's Underwriting Standards," a capitalized term defined nowhere, while Section 7(ee) measures origination by "the underwriting guidelines of the related originator." EMC did not originate these loans, so the two standards point to different documents.

The clause warrants that "no claims will arise as to broker fees that are double charged" — a promise about future third-party conduct rather than a statement of existing fact, made as of the Closing Date. What breach of a warranty about future claims would look like is left open.

The proviso caps lost note affidavits at "no more than 1% of the Revolving Credit Loans, in the aggregate," while Section 4(b)(iii) permits the Seller to deliver lost note affidavits in lieu of Mortgage Notes for every loan identified on Exhibit 5, without any percentage limit. The delivery accommodation and the warranty cap conflict.

This warrants that the Mortgage Note, Mortgage, Assignment and Exhibit 1 documents "have been delivered to the Purchaser or its designee," while Section 4(b) requires delivery to the Indenture Trustee or the Custodian on its behalf. Whether delivery to the Custodian satisfies a warranty of delivery to the Purchaser has to be construed.

The warranty that no "solid wastes" exist on any Mortgaged Property, as that term is defined in RCRA, is literally breached by ordinary household refuse on any residential lot. The absolute, unqualified scope of the term is what a court would be asked to cabin.

This repeats the disclosure warranty already made in Section 7(rr) and adds a forward-looking duty that "[t]he Servicer shall maintain such statement in the Servicing File," although the Servicer is not a party to this Agreement. The overlap with 7(rr) and the covenant on a non-party leave its operative effect unclear.

The warranty turns on "LTV," "CLTV" and "Equity LTV," none of which is defined in this Agreement, and the Section 1 definition of "Value" (the lesser of appraised value and sales price) is never tied to them. The ratios warranted cannot be computed from the instrument.

For second lien loans the Seller warrants it has received no "notice of default of a junior lien," although a second lienholder's exposure is to default under the senior lien, as Section 7(s)(3) recognizes by referring to encumbrances "senior to each Mortgage." "Junior" appears to be an error for "senior," and as written the warranty protects nothing.

"[N]o Mortgagor was encouraged or required to select" a higher-cost product uses an unmeasurable verb — what counts as encouragement by a loan officer is nowhere fixed — and the exception turns on "debit-to-income ratios," a misspelling of debt-to-income. The scope of the steering warranty cannot be determined from the words.

The warranty that underwriting "confirmed that at the time of origination, the Mortgagor had a reasonable ability to make timely payments" states no benchmark — no ratio, no documentation standard, no period over which ability is measured. On a stated-income revolving line that phrase is the whole battleground.

"[N]o Revolving Credit Loan is subject to negative amortization" cannot be squared with Section 7(w), which requires each title policy to contain "all applicable endorsements including a negative amortization endorsement, if applicable." If no loan negatively amortizes, the endorsement requirement is inexplicable.

The Seller warrants that "the Servicer has fully furnished ... accurate and complete information" to the three repositories on a monthly basis, although the Servicer is a non-party (GreenPoint) whose conduct EMC does not control, and no period is stated over which the monthly reporting is warranted. Both the actor and the time frame are left open.

The representations are said to inure to the Purchaser "its successors and assigns," while the sole-remedy paragraph that follows names only the Purchaser, the Indenture Trustee and the Noteholders and the Insurance and Indemnity Agreement makes the Note Insurer a third-party beneficiary of the Operative Documents. Whether the Note Insurer takes the benefit of these warranties as an assign is left to be construed across the documents.

The trigger states two different thresholds in one sentence: a breach "which materially and adversely affects the value of the interests of the Purchaser, the Noteholders, the Indenture Trustee or the Note Insurer ... or which adversely affects the interests of the Note Insurer." Whether the Note Insurer must show materiality at all, having been named in both limbs, is squarely presented by the words.

Cure, repurchase or substitution is made "the sole and exclusive remedy," yet Section 2.02(n) of the Insurance and Indemnity Agreement independently obliges the Sponsor to defend and indemnify the Insurer against all losses arising from the same breach of this Section 7. Whether the sole-remedy clause caps the Insurer's recovery under the Insurance Agreement is the central relational question of this transaction.

The provision defers accrual of a cause of action until discovery of the breach and a failure to cure, repurchase or substitute, although the representations themselves are made "as of the Closing Date" and are either true or false then. Whether parties can postpone accrual this way, and what "discovery" means, is exactly what such a clause invites a court to decide.

Paragraph (a) is a lead-in containing no representation and paragraph (b) begins the substance, so the lettering of the Section 8 warranties is displaced by one throughout. The section is also captioned "Concerning the HELOC Seller" here while the table of contents calls it "Concerning EMC."

The exception ends "and, in connection with the recordation of the Mortgages, powers of attorney or assignments of Mortgages not yet completed" — a dangling phrase with no verb, so what is being excepted from the no-consents representation is not stated. The mechanical incompleteness changes the reach of the warranty.

The second limb reaches only proceedings which "in the judgment of the HELOC Seller" could reasonably be expected to be determined adversely, making the seller's own judgment the measure of its disclosure obligation. Nothing in the clause fixes an objective standard against which that judgment could be tested.

"HELOC Seller's Information" is said to be defined in Section 13(a), the indemnification section, while Exhibit 3 to this Agreement is itself titled "HELOC Seller's Information." Which text fixes the scope of the information warranted has to be resolved between the two.

The disclosure of threatened proceedings is limited to those which "in the judgment of the Purchaser" could reasonably be expected to be determined adversely, leaving the Purchaser to set the threshold of its own warranty. No objective benchmark is supplied.

"Purchaser's Information" is said to be defined in Section 13(b), the indemnification section, while Exhibit 4 to this Agreement is separately titled "Purchaser's Information." The two possible sources of the definition are not reconciled.

This makes the Purchaser's obligations subject to the conditions "set forth in Section 10," but Section 2(a) conditions the purchase and sale on "the conditions set forth in Section 11 hereof" while Section 2(c) refers to Section 10. Which section states the conditions to closing is stated inconsistently across the Agreement.

The condition requires the Purchaser to have received "all of the following closing documents," but no list of documents follows the colon in the instrument, and the forms need only be "agreed upon and reasonably acceptable to the Purchaser." As written, neither the documents nor the standard for their sufficiency can be identified.
